name: Palewyami / Paleuyami
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Kroeber, A. L. 1963. Yokuts Dialect Survey. Anthropological Records 11(3): 177-252. Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press.
catalog_locator: §431 'Palewyami', 'Sound Correspondences', p. 232; §140 'Phonetic Insufficiencies', p. 182; §421 'The Yokuts Numeral Count', p. 230 (s.v. 'Ten', 'Three'); orthography note (acute = stress) p. 179; §340 'Tribal Names in Eleven Dialects', p. 224; §341.1 'Vowel Change or Epenthesis with Stress', p. 226
catalog_quote: Sound Correspondences. General Yokuts i often > e in Paleuyami, e > i, and u > o, o > u. These shifts are most frequent in the stressed penult, sometimes involve the final syllable, but only occasionally the first syllable if there are three. When i and e, or again u and o, occur in the same word, there is thus an effect of vowel inversion by metathesis in Paleuyami. Frequent also is stressed a > e. [p. 232] ... As for stress, one of my notebooks of 1906 contains an entry that stress falls so regularly on the penult, that unmarked forms can be assumed to carry it there. If nevertheless my vocabularies show antepenult or final stress more frequently than the examples in Newman's description, I lay this partly to actual aberrances from rule in the remoter dialects with which Newman could no longer work, and more largely to unintended deviations by informants in pronouncing isolated words. I think stress is one of the features of speech which I hear better than most features, as I hear tone level or shift worse. [p. 182] ... Three. The basic form seems to be co pi'n. Poso Creek was recorded as co pi'-the surd n may have been missed. ... Ten. I wrote this as tieu and t'ieu. The latter is right. Of seventeen times that I added stress accents, fifteen were on the first vowel. As Yokuts stress is on the penult, the final u must be a consonant [p. 230]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Kroeber states this as the general Yokuts rule (p. 182, p. 231: 'As Yokuts stress is on the penult') and, in the Palewyami-specific section, treats the penult as 'the stressed penult' when describing where Palewyami's vowel shifts occur, i.e. he takes Palewyami to follow the penultimate pattern. Non-penult stress marks in his 1903/1906 Palewyami list (e.g. co pi' 'three') he attributes to hearing errors, missed final consonants, or informant over-emphasis.
new_statements.exceptions: For Yokuts generally: antepenult stress is 'exceptional in Yokuts' but occurs in plurals of tribal names (p. 226-227); Kroeber concedes 'actual aberrances from rule in the remoter dialects' (p. 182) without specifying Palewyami; Poso Creek 'three' recorded with final stress (co pi'), explained as a missed final n (p. 231).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms elicited for a c. 300-item vocabulary from a single semi-speaker (Mrs. Solto, who learned the language from her grandmother), 1903 and 1906; no texts, no connected speech; Kroeber (1907: 183) notes for Yaudanchi that word accent tends to give way to phrase accent in connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Kroeber 1963 calls the variety Palewyami / Paleuyami (informant's own name Peleuyi) of Poso Creek, Kern County; Glottolog pale1254 'Palewyami Yokuts' is the same variety (CLA: Yokuts > Poso Creek Yokuts > Palewyami). The Palewyami-specific stress statement is only a presupposition ('the stressed penult') inside a section on vowel correspondences; the explicit rule (p. 182, p. 231) is stated for Yokuts as a whole, from Kroeber's 1906 notebooks covering all his dialects including Palewyami. Nothing in Newman 1944 or later phonological work covers Palewyami, which was extinct before Newman's fieldwork.

new_statements.quote: [p. 28, §4:1] Stress is well marked in Yokuts. Words are regularly accented on the penult. Exceptions to this mechanical stress occur in a) words whose final syllable contains the durative -xo’ (§6:10) [...] and in b) a few three-syllable nouns having a strong vowel in the first syllable. Such words are stressed on the antepenult [...] A group of words composing a phrase is pronounced as a stress unit, taking the stress on the penultimate syllable. [...] [p. 29] But word stress will be marked on words in which the mechanical rule of penultimate stress is violated; unmarked words will be understood as having the regular penultimate stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (penult) and same type (fixed, non-contrastive) as the catalog record for Palewyami (Kroeber 1963: 'stressed penult', stress falls regularly on the penult). Adds detail the catalog lacks (antepenult exception classes a/b, phrase stress, marking convention), but the agreement is at the general-Yokuts level only: Newman's grammar is built on six dialects (Yawelmani, Chukchansi, Gashowu, Choynimni, Chawchila, Wikchamni) and contains no Palewyami/Poso Creek forms -- HTRC EF tokens show no 'Paleuyami'/'Palewyami' anywhere in the volume and 'Poso Creek' only once, p. 220, in an ethnonym list ('Poso Creek People'). The Palewyami-specific evidence of record remains Kroeber 1963 §431…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yokuts word stress is non-contrastive ('mechanical') and falls regularly on the penultimate syllable. Two lexical/morphological exception classes take antepenultimate stress: (a) words whose final syllable is the durative suffix -xo' (Yawelmani present durative; Gashowu -xV and Choynimni -xo' aorist durative), a relic of that suffix's former enclitic status (in Chawchila the suffix has been reintegrated and such words have leveled to normal stress; per section 6:10, where the suffix has full syllabic value the word takes normal penultimate stress); (b) a few trisyllabic nouns with a strong vowel in the first syllable (e.g. the word for 'dog' in Gashowu/Choynimni). Phrase stress: a phrase is a stress unit stressed on its penultimate syllable, with nouns and verbs keeping their word stress unmodified as phrase nucleus. Newman marks stress only where the penultimate rule is violated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the readable fragments of section 4 (gaps remain in the extract; the EF token list for pp. 28-29 shows no 'secondary' token)
new_statements.exceptions: (a) words ending in the durative -xo' (Yawelmani present durative, Gashowu/Choynimni aorist durative) -> antepenult, leveled to regular penult in Chawchila; (b) a few three-syllable nouns with a strong first-syllable vowel -> antepenult; phrase-level: particles/pronouns lose stress to the phrase nucleus (fragment B, partly gapped).
new_statements.identity_note: Newman 1944 describes 'Yokuts' from six dialects -- Yawelmani (principal), Chukchansi, Gashowu, Choynimni, Chawchila, Wikchamni -- all Valley/Foothill Yokuts; Palewyami (Poso Creek), the divergent southern Yokutsan variety catalogued as pale1254, is not among his sources and is mentioned only as an ethnonym (p. 220). His stress rule is framed as pan-Yokuts; its application to Palewyami is by family-level generalisation, corroborated independently by Kroeber 1963's Palewyami notes.

sources.note: 'Accent and enclitics' pp. 182-183 is about Yaudanchi (Tule-Kaweah), not Palewyami: 'Stress accent of separate words is not very marked.. Unsuffixed words without long vowels most frequently are accented on the penult, sometimes on the antepenult'; p. 190 'the accent is on the penultimate vowel or diphthong unless specially indicated'. The Paleuyami section pp. 347-352 treats only vowel differentiation/assimilation/metathesis and says nothing about accent. Comparative note p. 333: hummingbird names in all dialects accented on the first syllable.
